messages.subject: Re: left truncation and h(0)
messages.body_plain:
> > Any thoughts on using a left truncation if the detection PDF starts low
> > and peaks about 10 m out?   I'm using that this is either due to evasive
> > movements or a road effect or both.  If I do use a left truncation, how
> > does this affect density estimates?
> >
> > Also,  what are acceptable values for h(0)?  I'm guessing that it should
> > be very small - is that correct?

I'm assuming this is point transect sampling.  If the effect is evasive
movement, you should not left-truncate - by keeping the 'hole' in the
data, the lack of detections within 10m averages out with the excess at
around 10m.  If you left-truncate, you overestimate densities.  If the
effect is because there is no habitat close to the point because it is on
a road, then left-truncation is OK.  You then estimate the density of
birds in the habitat bordering the road - and you must hope that that is
representative of habitat more generally.  My own view is that point
transects should not be positioned along roads.  The habitat along the
road is very unlikely to be representative for a variety of reasons.  For
example, if the road passes through woodland, it creates edge habitat,
which tends to have higher bird densities.  Point transects positioned
along roads simply estimate density along roads, which isn't usually what
you want to measure.  This is one of the problems of the North American
Breeding Bird Survey - it is unsurprising that most species of deep forest
are in decline on the sample plots when those plots are positioned along
roads.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'm working on some SAS macros to run DISTANCE in batch mode to analyse
some ungrouped line transect data I've collected. As part of this I want to
answer the question whether I can pool the data of four strata to get a
pooled estimate for f(0). I'm using the likelihood ratio test described on
page 374 in the 1993 distance book for this. The problem I encounterd here
is that the test statistic I get depends on the truncation distance I
selected, even when the number of observations stays the same (as an
extreme example: truncation distance is larger that the largest observed
distance). The reason for this is obviously the sligthly changing lnLs for
the pooled and strata datasets. As far as I understood this is an effect of
the normalizing function (y_s = y/w) mentioned on page 59 (2001 book). Is
this correct? And: How do I have to set the truncation distances for the
pooled and strata datasets to get reliable results for the likelihood ratio
test. (a) Do I have to use the same fixed value which is equal to or lower
than the largest observed distance in the pooled dataset for the pooled and
the strata-wise analyses even if the largest distance of a particular
stratum is (possibly much) lower than this value or (b) do I have to use
this value only for the pooled analysis and set a single truncation
distance for each stratum which is equal to the largest distance of that
stratum but lower than or equal to the truncation distance of the pooled
dataset? In my case this seems to be quite crucial as the first option
results in accepting the null hypothesis while the second one rejects it.
Moreover the respective p-values are very different (ca. 0.19 and 0.003).

Many thanks in advance

        Felix

Applied Computer Science

messages.subject: Re: different lnL for different truncation distances
messages.subject_clean: different lnL for different truncation distances
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felix, list:

Firstly, I would tend to use AIC rather than LR tests to decide whether to pool
or not (assuming you're most interested in the global density estimate; if
you're interested in the stratum level estimates then better not to pool if you
have enough data to reliably estimate by stratum).  I'm sure you have a good
reason for using the LR tests though, so...

Different truncation distances will indeed change the LR test results, because
changing the truncation distance means you've changed the data, even if the
number of observations doesn't change.  As an example, say you have a large
number of observations and your distance is 200 meters.  If you truncate at 500
meters, you're telling the estimation algorithm that you saw nothing between 200
and 500 meters - so there is considerable evidence that the detection function
is be close to zero in that interval.  If, however, you truncate at 200 meters,
there is no evidence at all about the detection function between 200 and 500
meters -- so the fitted detection function will probably be a bit different.  To
put it a different way, seeing nothing within a given interval is data too!

Regarding truncation for the pooled and by stratum analysis, you must truncate
the same way for both -- otherwise you aren't making a fair comparison
(different data).

I was interested to hear that you're using SAS macros to run Distance.  If you'd
be willing to send a zip file containing the macros, an example dataset and some
brief instructions, I can post them on the web site to give other people and
example of how to do this.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think the email below answers my question on how to model and predict
detectability using landscape features; right ? Originally, I would have
done it externally as a GLM, or so, and in R/SPLUS using slope, aspect,
landcover...

My second question deals with finding the best left truncation width:

We have many aerial survey transects, and they all have different
'closest detection widths' from the flight line for each transect, e.g.
100m, 80m, 85m etc.

What would be suggested to find the 'best' left truncation width, e.g.
when pooling across transects or when analyzing for each transect: mean,
min, max, or manual trial and error ?
Should that be modeled even ?

The assumption is that the left truncation is required due to the
blocked down-view in the plane (no glass bottom), but not due to a g(0)
problem.

The less left truncation the 'better' the f(0), right ?

Is there anything else to be considered ?

Thanks for any hints and suggestions; best regards

   F.

Falk Huettmann
Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA
Email ff...@uaf.edu  Phone 907 474 7882 Fax 907 474 6716

-----Original Message-----
From: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] On Behalf Of Len Thomas
Sent: Thursday, May 13, 2004 10:05 PM
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Adjusting counts for detectability and
covariates

Hi James,

I don't think you need to do anything by hand, unless you're a
masochist!    I
wasn't 100% clear in my previous message so I'll try to lay it out
better here.
For that reason I'm also cc'ing this to the list, in case anyone else
wants to
do the same thing.

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but
with
habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the
probability
of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the point and that
the
animal is present within the truncation distance.  You then want to
calculate
density (or abundance) at each point using this habitat-specific
probability of
detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the
Model
Definition | Estimate tab.  Under "Quantities to estimate and level of
resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both
the
"Global" and "Sample" columns.  Make sure you have habitat as a
covariate.  For
more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining MCDS models,
Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.

The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for
animals at
each point too.  (You will also get abundance for each point, but
there's a bug
in Distance where the area used to calculate this is currently wrong so
it's
acutally abunance for the whole study area assuming density at that
point
applies to the whole study area -- this bug is fixed in the next version
of
Distance to be released.)

You *can* calculate probability of detection by hand if you really want
to - but
it's going to require some work.  We want p_i, the probability of
detecting an
animal at each point, given that it is within the truncation distance.
Note,
this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at it's observed
distance --
it's the probability given that the animal was somewhere between 0 and
w.  We
could use the observed distances but then estimation tends to be less
reliable
-- for more on this see the MCDS chapter of the up-coming Advanced
Distance
Sampling book.  Because we're integrating out the distance component,
the only
covariate left is habitat, so that means the p_i's will be the same for
all
animals at each point, given the amount of shrub cover.  So what you
need to do
is program Excel (or something better) to work out probability of
detection for
a given covariate level and distance, and then program Excel (or
whatever) to
integrate this function between 0 and w, using numerical integration
such as
Simpson's rule.  As you can see, it's probably easier to let Distance do
it!

Specific replies to your questions about estimating p below, should you
still
want to do it.

Cheers,

 - Len

On Thu, 13 May 2004 14:58:43 -0400, Tucker, James wrote:

> >Dr. Thomas:
> >
> >Thank you for replying to my question.  I tried to estimate density by
sample,
but I do not have enough observations for most samples (points) to
estimate
probability of detection for individual points.  Could you please help
me with
the following questions?
> >
> >If I calculate p_i, the estimated probability of detecting the ith
animal, will
the mean for the p_i at a point be a good estimate for probability of
detection
at that point?

As I explained above, you could do it this way, but better to use the
definition
I gave of p_i as probability of detection given the animal is between 0
and w,
rather than probability at a given distance.  In the former case, all
p_i's for
each animal at a point are the same (because you have no animal level
covariates
other than distance).

> >I do not have animal level covariates, but I want to adjust p_i to
account for
the influence of shrub cover at each point.  Does the calculation of "s"
in the
equation below include measurements for shrub cover at the individual
points?

Yes.

> >Effort        :    86.00000

> > # samples     :    86

> > Width         :    100.0000

> > # observations:   297

> >

> > Model

> >    Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(2))

> >

> >    s = A(1) * Exp(fcn(A(3)))

> >    Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.

> >    Parameter A(2) is the power parameter.

> >    Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of covariate ARCSHRUB.

> >

> >

> >              Point        Standard    Percent Coef.        95 Percent

> >  Parameter   Estimate       Error      of Variation     Confidence
Interval

> >  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------
----------------------

> >    A( 1)      80.60        2.078

> >    A( 2)      9.000        6.475

> >    A( 3)     0.9226E-13   0.1306

> >    h(0)     0.27274E-03  0.82188E-05       3.01      0.25704E-03
0.28940E-03

> >  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------
----------------------

> >In the above equation for "s", what is "fcn"?  I plan to use an Excel
spreadsheet to do the calculations.  I am somewhat mathematically
challenged, so
it would be great if you know Excel and can tell me the function in
Excel that
corresponds to "fcn".

Fcn is short for function.  It's a bit obscure I agree.  Your shrub
covariate is
a non-factor covariate - let's denote it's value at a particular point
as z.
Then to evaluate Exp(fcn(A(3))), you calculate Exp(z*A(3)).  So,
overall:
k(y)= 1 - Exp(-(y/[A(1)*exp(z*A(3))])**-A(2))

> >In the following equation for probability of detection,
g(y)=key(y)[1+series
(y)]/key(0)[1+series(0)] what parameters do I use to calculate
series(y)?  The
example in Distance/Help uses A(3), but that example does not include a
covariate.

You didn't have any series expansion terms in your model, judging from
your
output above.  In this case k(0)=1, so you don't need the bottom line so
k(y)=g
(y).

As an aside, the above parameter estimates appear to indicate that there
is very
little effect of the habitat covariate (A(3), unless your habitat values
are
very large numbers.  For example, if z=1x10^11, then exp(z*A(3)) is
1.00926.
Did AIC really select this model over one with no covariates?  Also, the
values
of A(1) and A(2) seem to indicate a wide shoulder and then a steep drop
off --
although "wide" is relative to the scale of your measurements.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.body_plain:
Falk, list,

> >I think the email below answers my question on how to model and predict
> >detectability using landscape features; right ? Originally, I would have
> >done it externally as a GLM, or so, and in R/SPLUS using slope, aspect,
> >landcover...

Yes indeed.  The useful feature that Distance offers over the above programmable
software is the built-in ability to include adjustment terms in the detection
function (not straightforward to program); the downside of the current MCDS
engine in Distance is that it is hard to add interaction terms (you have to
manually add another field/fields that code the interaction).  The new MRDS
(mark-recapture distance sampling) engine, which will be available in the next
version of Distance, allows interactions but at present doesn't offer adjustment
terms.  One day, however, I hope we'll implement both in the same engine!

> >My second question deals with finding the best left truncation width:

> >We have many aerial survey transects, and they all have different
> >'closest detection widths' from the flight line for each transect, e.g.
> >100m, 80m, 85m etc.

I'm not clear (1) whether the distances are measured as exact or in intervals --
I suspect exact; (2) whether you expect the view to be obsured beneath the plane
to a different extent on different transects (e.g., because of flying at
different altitudes relative to the ground).  If, for example, there is no
reason to suppose the amount of obsuring to vary between transcts then there is
no reason to truncate differently on different transects.  This would be good,
because otherwise you'd need to do the analysis outside of Distance (which only
supports one common truncation distance for all the data).

> >What would be suggested to find the 'best' left truncation width, e.g.
> >when pooling across transects or when analyzing for each transect: mean,
> >min, max, or manual trial and error ?
> >Should that be modeled even ?

The best option is to go back to the conditions on the plane and try to work out
a truncation distance at which there was no obsuring of the view.  Looking at
the data, for the mode (high point of the histogram) will give an indication -
but some obscuring could already be taking place at that point.

If you're flying at different altitudes and the altitude is recorded, and the
data are in intervals, then a only small modification to the standard fitting
algorithm for interval data is needed.  I've been interested in this for a while
but never found time (or funds) to get it into the analysis engines.

> >The assumption is that the left truncation is required due to the
> >blocked down-view in the plane (no glass bottom), but not due to a g(0)
> >problem.

> >The less left truncation the 'better' the f(0), right ?

Having left truncated, you have two options: (1) fit a detection function to the
truncated data as is.  This does not assume that g(x)=1 at the truncation point.
(2) subtract the truncation distance from all data -- effectively move the
centreline out to be ą the truncation distance.  This then assumes that g(x)=1
at the truncation distance.  The former strategy has a weaker assumption, but
will give higher variance as the detection function close to the line has no
data to tell it where to fit -- it will be relying on the data from > the left
truncation point and the assumed shape of the detection function.

> >Is there anything else to be considered ?

In general, I wonder if even when collecting exact distances from a plane, it's
worth having lines taped on the window and on the outside of the plane that
indicate a left truncation point to the observers.  They can record animals seen
inside this line if they wish (always allow observers to record data that can
then be truncated later), but they should concentrate on seeing all animals at
the truncation line and further out from the plane.  That way you know where to
left truncate at the analysis stage, and the observers know where they should be
concentrating their effort.  Practical aspects of data collection are not my
strong point, so let's see if anyone else comes up with something useful there.

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: sample density estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff, list,

Thanks for sending me your project file.  Using it, I could pinpoint the problem.
To recap, you are using the MCDS engine to fit a covariate that differs for each
point.  You want to fit a global detection function with this covariate, but then
predict density at each point using the covariate level specific to that point.
The way you do this in Distance is to tick the following boxes in the "Quantities
to estimate and levels of resolution" section of the Estimate tab of your Model
Definition:
- in the Density row, tick the Sample column (you want density for each sample)
- in the Detection function row, you tick *both* the Global column and the Sample
column.  You want Distance to fit a global detection function, but estimate the
detection probability by sample.  (You had only ticked the Global column, so it
was applying the same detection function to all samples, regardless of their
covariate value.)

This is documented in Chapter 9 of the online manual under "Estimating the
detection function at multiple levels" and there is an example and screen shot in
the Program Reference Appendix under Model Definition | Estimate.  I'll add
another screen shot and example to Chapter 9 to help make it clearer.

As an aside, I notice that your covariate is defined at the observation level,
with the same value for each observation within a sample (point).  When the
covariate more naturally attaches to the sample, you can define it at the sample
level.  Same goes for stratum-level covariates.  Won't affect the results -- just
less data to import.

I'll return the project file with an example under separate cover.

 - Len

--

messages.subject_clean: Correcting for detection probability - at the species level or
messages.body_plain:
I have data from transect surveys of birds during migration in which
detections were recorded into three distance (0-5m, 5-10m, and 10-25m)
classes from the transect line (500m long) among 24 transects (of two
treatments) in riverine forests.  Each transect was sampled 20 times per
season for two autumns.  Originally, we had hoped that detection
probabilities would not be significantly different from 1 so that we
didn=92t need to make adjustments for detection and treat the surveys as
strip transects.  However, when I computed detection functions for all
birds combined for individual transects by pooling all 40 replicate
samples for each transect (generally >200 observations per transect), I
found that 58% of the transects had detection probabilities less than one
(ranging from 0.63 to .90).  This makes me think it is worth my time to
make an abundance adjustment to the data for each sample to improve the
accuracy of the data.

and all birds combined.  My question is at what organizational level do I

messages.subject: Re: Correcting for detection probability - at the species level
messages.subject_clean: Correcting for detection probability - at the species level
messages.body_plain:
Jeff, we generally recommend that you fit detection functions at the
species level.  However, if all you need is abundance of all species
combined, it is OK to pool across species - that gives you a good estimate
of total abundance, but poor (biased) estimates of abundance by species.
This doesn't assume all species have the same detection function - it
relies on 'pooling robustness'.  However, I would exclude any species that
are expected to be unusual in terms of detectability - e.g. exceptionally
cryptic species.  Using the covariate model can help with rare species
relative to fitting each species independently, allowing you to include a
few more species in your analysis, but very rare species will remain
problematic.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: problems with Coverage Probability
messages.body_plain:
Hi Barbara, (cc list - if you're not interested in GIS issues in Distance then
don't bother reading this!)

Thank-you for sending your project file.  A number of issues:

- At present, there are no spatial analysis capabilties within Distance, so
there is no reason to import GIS data into distance if all you want to do is
analyze your data.  Therefore, there is no reason to import your transect data.
The geographic capabilities inside Distance are currently limited to survey
design, and for this you need shapefiles for the study area and any strata you
want to define.  If you're intersted in both analysis of current data and design
of a future survey, I suggest you do this in two separate projects -- one non-
geographic project for the analysis, and a geographic one for the design.

- I had a quick look at the shapefiles you sent in ArcMap, and it seems clear
that your transects were not randomly located, but are probably trails or such
like.  I expect you're aware of the limitations of using trails (see the
distance sampling text book, or look back in the archives of this list).

- Okay, let's concentrate on how to set up a project for survey design.  The
project you sent didn't work because you didn't have the GIS data imported
correctly.  I'll walk you through it below, and send a copy of an example
project in a separate email.

Your survey area is composed of two separate regions, and you sent me a
shapefile with these regions stored as two polygons.  So, I guess you'll want a
project with a global data layer and a stratum data layer with 2 records.

How to do this:
First thing I did was to create such a project in Distance.  I chose File | New
project, then gave it a name, then chose the option to "Design a new survey" and
clicked finish.  This created the Global layer (called "study area" by default)
with one record in it.  In the data tab, I then chose to create a new layer, and
created a stratum layer which I called region.  I then added two records to this
layer by clicking on the empty ID record for the layer and clicking the Insert
Record button twice.

Because your shapefiles are already projected, I didn't bother telling Distance
about the projection -- this means it will work with the x,y data without doing
any on-the-fly projections to it, which is exactly what you want.  The default
units when there are no proejctions are meters (see File | Project properties |
Geographic) so there's nothign to do there.  For more about this, look in the
online help index under "Projection" - there's a page you'll find called
"Coordinate systems, maps and calculations in Distance" which suggests importing
already projected data in this way.

- Now I need to import the GIS data. First thing is to see what shapefiles I
need to create.  If I select the "Study area" layer, and choose the menu item
"Data | Data layer properties" and look in the geographic tab, I can see it has
an attached shapefile called "Study_ar" in the project's data folder.  By doing
the same thing for the "Region" layer, I can see there's also a shapefile called
"Region".  I'm going to replace these empty shapefiles with your GIS data.

Instructions on how to do this are in the online manual - look in the index
under GIS data | Importing.  Here's what I did to follow them:

I closed the Distance project.  Then in the GIS package ArcMap, I opened the
shapefile you sent with the two region polygons in it.  As documented in the
help pages, I made sure your attribute table had a field called LinkID, and that
the numbers in it were sequential 1, 2.  Then I exported this shapefile right
over the top of the "Region" shapefile in the Distance project's data folder.
Now for the global layer - that one must have only one polygon in it.  So I
edited the shapefile you sent and merged the two polygons into one multi-part
polygon.  I made sure the LinkID was 1.  I then exported this over the top of
the "Study_ar" polygon in the data layer.  Done!

I now opened the Distance project again, and created a Map in the Maps tab,
adding the two data layers to check they were there okay.  Another way to check
the data is to click on the word "Polygon" for each record in the Data tab.

Next thing to do, before designing any surveys, is create a coverage probability
grid.  I created a new data layer, and set the type to Coverage.  Under
properties, I set the grid spacing to 100 meters (a good spacing is about your
truncation distance -- but I didn't know what that was, and didn't want to
create too many grid points as it can take a long time).

Then you're ready to go.  I created an example systematic line survey to get you
started.

I'll send the project file, zipped up, under separate cover.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ
